messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rodrigo is a 62-year-old married Latin American man who has spent most of his adult life as a professional dancer and choreographer. He came to the clinic eight months after a life-threatening motor vehicle collision in which he was broadsided at high speed by a driver who ran a red light. The impact caved in the driver's side door, and Rodrigo was trapped in the wreckage for nearly forty minutes before emergency crews cut him free. What lodged most deeply in him was not the initial crash but the sounds — the grinding shriek of metal, the hiss of the deployed airbag, a car alarm cycling on and off in the silence afterward — and the absolute inability to move his body, the instrument he had trusted for four decades. He lay pinned, certain he was about to die, and he could not do a single thing to prevent it.

In the months that followed, Rodrigo found that the event resisted language entirely. He could not tell his wife what had happened in any way that felt true; the experience sat in him as sensation and sound rather than story, fragmented and without sequence. When memories surfaced — and they surfaced without warning — he would hear the metal shriek again, feel the airbag's chemical sting in his nostrils, and with those sensory echoes came a wave of intense shame that surprised him and that he struggled to account for. He had come to believe, quietly and with great conviction, that the crash had happened because of the kind of man he was — that some flaw in his character, some accumulated carelessness or pride, had made him deserving of it. This belief that the event reflected something essential about him meant that the world now felt permanently dangerous: if his own nature had drawn disaster once, it would draw it again. He was certain that bad things would keep happening to him and that he was powerless to stop them. That helplessness settled into his body as a constant low hum of threat, and he began scanning every room he entered for exits the moment he walked through the door — a habit his students at the dance studio noticed before he did. He startled violently when a colleague touched his shoulder to get his attention during a rehearsal, and the shame of that visible flinch in front of younger dancers compounded the belief that something was fundamentally broken in him.

Because the memories arrived with such physical force — the auditory replays, the shame, the bodily terror — Rodrigo began working to prevent them. He started suppressing any thought that edged toward the crash, pushing it down the moment it surfaced. He discovered that staying awake until two or three in the morning kept him too exhausted to ruminate, and he began deliberately dissociating during the day, teaching choreography in a kind of blurred detachment, watching himself from a slight distance as though his body were a student he was correcting. These strategies brought brief relief but steadily worsened his relationship with his own memory: the event became more fragmented, less narratable, more lodged in the body. The deliberate blanking-out meant he was never fully present with the memories long enough to process them, and the fragments that broke through felt more alien and more shameful each time. The suppression and dissociation also reinforced his sense that he was a man who could not cope, could not feel normally, could not be trusted with his own inner life — which fed directly back into his conviction that he was helpless and essentially damaged, keeping his threat system perpetually primed. He remained hypervigilant in the studio, scanning the mirrors for movement near the entrance, bracing at every unexpected sound, and that vigilance pulled the fragmented sensory memories closer to the surface, so that teaching a simple combination could suddenly be interrupted by the sound of metal in his head.

What finally brought Rodrigo to the clinic was a conversation with his wife, who told him gently that she felt she had lost him — that he was present in the house but absent from their life together. He arrived hoping, more than anything, to feel like himself again, and terrified that he no longer knew who that was.
